what: The faster the scroll, the more the middle of the photo panel sags (top·bottom edges bow like an arch) and the side lines curve, and the red·green channels split up and down (chromatic aberration). Speed is the difference from a value that follows the scroll position by 10% each frame, so it relaxes slowly when scrolling stops (three.js plane 300×300 cells). By default it is drawn on one screen-fixed canvas with a 60° perspective camera, so the bowed edges go outside the cell, and with stage: local it is clipped inside the cell.

options.stage: fixed (default — one screen-fixed canvas, behind the text) · local (canvas inside the cell, does not go outside the cell)
options.lerp: Follow ratio, default .1 — the smaller it is, the longer the lag lingers
options.sag: Center sag strength (share of board height per 1px of speed), default .0003
options.sway: Side-edge bend frequency (per 1px of speed), default .0001
options.amp: Side-edge bend amount (share of panel width), default .3
options.split: Color split (speed per 1px as uv), default .00005 — 0 turns it off
options.--fx-sag-layer: z-index of the fixed canvas, default -1 (behind text). If body paints the background it gets covered, so paint the background on html

use: Or — three.cjs is loaded between three-pre.js and three-post.js in this folder
note: The original’s hero photo measures the canvas size (getBoundingClientRect) at the moment the loader scales it to 1.3x, so the photo looks 1.3x larger and stuck to the top left. That quirk is tangled up with the site loader, so this motion part measures the frame’s layout size instead (the brand copy of shared.js keeps the original behaviour)

from.where: shared.js photo scroll distortion — two info photos (stage: fixed), hero and stylist photos (stage: local)
